title: 🎙️ Repair Culture & Practical Tech
description: Today is about things you can fix, keep running, and pass on — repair culture, right-to-repair wins and setbacks, gear that outlives its manufacturer's support window, and the maker ethos of building to last rather than building to replace. We're interested in tools, devices, and projects where longevity, repairability, and self-sufficiency intersect, especially in rural and off-grid contexts where you can't just run to a repair shop. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Repair Culture & Practical Tech' — the right to repair movement, gear that outlasts its manufacturer, DIY fixes, and tools built for longevity.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical conflict; natural disasters without an engineering or preparedness angle; wildlife and conservation; working-lands policy; Indigenous governance; science discoveries with no DIY or hardware relevance; financial market news.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Hands-on hardware journalism counts fully even without an explicit right-to-repair hook.
- 80-100: Directly about repairability — right-to-repair legislation wins and losses, iFixit-style teardowns scoring repairability, gear designed for user serviceability, products outliving manufacturer support and how owners keep them running, permacomputing, vintage hardware still in active use, open-source hardware, Rossmann-style repair advocacy, 3D-printed replacement parts, battery replacement guides, rural and off-grid repair self-sufficiency.
- 55-79: Hands-on maker and DIY content — builds, modifications, hardware hacks, workshop projects, practical electronics guides with real technical depth, 3D printing hardware and filament, off-grid and solar gear, home lab hardware, tools and workshop equipment, battery and power tech. Most genuine hands-on hardware journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Gadget and device reviews with some technical substance; consumer electronics touching software longevity or ecosystem lock-in; hardware whose selling point is open firmware or modular design.
- 10-29: Surface-level product announcements, gadget speculation, leaked specs, general tech news with no hardware or repair angle.

ANCHORS: 'Framework Laptop 16 teardown: a 9/10 repairability score' → 98. 'Oregon's right-to-repair law takes effect' → 92. 'Building a solar-powered Raspberry Pi weather station' → 68. 'Samsung teases thinner bezels on next Galaxy' → 15.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] How to support a colleague who has lost a loved one to suicide
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

In 2024 almost 50,000 Americans died by suicide, making it the 10th leading cause of death in the United States. And the ripple effects are even wider. According to research, each suicide is connected to 135 people who knew the deceased, including coworkers, along with a percentage of those who were considered “close connections.” Extrapolating that data, 6.6 million people are added to the larger community of suicide loss survivors each year.

I am one of those “loss survivors.” On January 5, 2025, while in a plane taxiing out on a runway, I received a text message from my half-brother telling me my father had died by suicide. The shock of his death, including how it was communicated, left me traumatized and depressed. While I was fortunate to have the strong support of my wife, daughter, and son-in-law, at some point I started to think, “Who should I tell?”

While the decision about sharing the loss of my father was highly personal and based on a number of factors, which I discussed with my grief therapist, it left me thinking, How can we support others in the workplace who have faced these unimaginable events in their lives? And that commitment is not one to be taken lightly, given the stigma of suicide, linked to effects that research lists as “concealment of the death, social withdrawal, reduced psychological and somatic functioning, and grief difficulties.”

The strategies here are designed as suggestions to help others who might want support but who might not ask for it. I would like to thank all of the mental health specialists and corporate leaders who agreed to be interviewed for this article.

I am not a mental health professional, and this is not mental health advice, but here are some approaches to your colleague who might not be ready, prepared, or equipped to share the grief and sense of loss that comes with the suicide of a loved one. 

Start with condolences

A good first step is to offer your condolences, delicately and respectfully. One person I interviewed, whose mother died by suicide, said, “A few of my colleagues handed me cards with handwritten notes of condolence. I will never forget how thoughtful that was, that they took the time to write a note of kindness.” I also experienced something similar, and will never forget those who took the time to be so mindful and respectful. Sure, email is always an option, but a deeper sense of sympathy is conveyed by a meaningful card with a handwritten note of condolences and support, beyond a simple signature.

By conveying condolences, without mentioning anything specific and respecting your colleague’s privacy, you allow the person who is grieving, as one mental health specialist stated, “to retain their own narrative without feeling like someone is being presumptive. Such gestures also convey availability and humanity without any assumption of a reply or explanation.” 

Offering further support

To gauge how to respond, you need to consider your relationship with the individual. Are they a colleague with whom you have little social connection other than work-related interactions, or a close coworker and friend you socialize with? How you decide to express your regrets should tie into that relationship.

If you don’t have a close relationship but work in the same office, a simple expression of regret or a note of support would be appreciated, demonstrating that even though you might not be particularly close, you care about your coworker and the death of their loved one. One person I interviewed told how such a work acquaintance sent a flower arrangement to their coworker’s desk, a touching gesture of support. “The fact that we were not particularly close, but he still took the time to send me some flowers, was extremely touching,” he said.

In the case of a close coworker, consider offering more support. As one corporate leader told me when such a coworker’s loved one died by suicide, “I didn’t want to just offer my condolences, I wanted to offer her my company, so I invited her to a tea outside the office, to give her a moment of respite from the stress of returning to work and to just take a break.” That invitation gave her colleague the liberty to share but without any imposition or intrusion. The corporate leader added, “My friend was just appreciative that I took her out of the office environment, and even for a brief moment, to feel that she could just converse and it didn’t have to be about her grief.”

However, keep in mind even a close colleague may not be prepared to talk about what happened. If a grieving colleague doesn’t want to engage, respect their boundaries. Especially shortly after someone’s death and the return to work,  there are strong reasons why your colleague might not want to engage more specifically, beyond accepting your condolences. Those reasons include:

  • Confusion around how the death occurred. “How could this have happened?”
  • Self-scrutiny and self-blame: “Should I have done more?”
  • Anger. “How could they have done that to us?”
  • Religious objections and guilt. 
  • Shame: “I never thought I would have this in my life.”

If your colleague does want more support 

Grief is a long and complicated journey. A colleague who may want privacy now may later approach you once they have had more time to process their grief, but only if you have conveyed your availability earlier. Here are some dos and don’ts to signal your wanting to keep the door open and render future support.  

Don’ts: These might close off any future conversations and possibilities to help.

  • Offer to talk if you don’t mean it. One person I interviewed had a colleague offer support, but when she replied months later, “Yes, I’d love to take you up on that virtual catch-up,” there was no reply. That added unnecessary hurt and isolation to what was already a difficult ask in reaching out.
  • Bring up the manner of death. A simple “If you ever want to chat and talk, just know that I am always here to support you” is empathetic while nonintrusive.
  • Make it about you. Saying something like, “I know what you are going through, the same thing happened in my family” shifts the narrative to yourself from the person you are trying to console. Worse, as one mental health professional told me, “Equating your own loss might make your colleague feel like you are minimizing theirs.” 
  • Rush in with early assurances such as, “Don’t worry, it’s going to be OK,” or, “You’re strong, you will get through it.” Your colleague is going through a period of uncertainty that needs to be understood, and empathetic listening is your best way to show support without offering what might be perceived as unhelpful counsel. 
  • Provide a reading list. There are an abundance of books on grief, some specifically pertaining to suicide. However, recommending a book can feel like an assignment, even if well intentioned. As one person I interviewed said, “It started to feel like a cascade of people offering condolences were telling me about a book that I really needed to read. It was overwhelming and also gave me anxiety as to what I should be reading, if at all.”  Recommending a book is on a very thin wire with respect to mental health counseling, so perhaps it’s not the time to signal, “Here’s what you should be doing.”

Do’s: These will signal a strong sense of future availability. 

  • If you are close to the person, and have a friendship that would be sustained even if you were not colleagues, open the door to the future. A simple “I am here if you ever want to talk,” conveys understanding and empathy, and also respects your friend’s sense of privacy. One colleague reached out to me with such an offer six months after my father’s suicide. His counsel was extremely helpful, but if he had made the offer sooner I would have been ill-prepared to accept the kind gesture. 
  • Be a steady listener. In your initial interaction with your colleague, allow them the narrative. Don’t try to finish sentences or overtake the conversation. Whatever they might share, replying with understanding and validation will demonstrate a strong sense of empathy that might be very helpful over time.
  • Offer resources, but prepare first. Many organizations offer a range of mental health support resources that can be helpful, including employee assistance programs and specific grief support and counseling access. One corporate leader explained that their company has trained mental health aides who are third-party certified to support those who are grieving. These are all helpful, but in your approach to your colleague, a good start might be, “I know we have good support and counseling resources here. If you need help finding them, or even if you want me to go to HR with you to help find where to start, just let me know.” That way, you are not overwhelming them with what might be multiple options, but just offering support without intrusion. 
  • Offer to talk outside the office. Taking someone out of the office can offer a sense of intimacy without the pressure of office interactions. With such outreach, you are offering what might be the most important thing you can offer: your undivided companionship. And it doesn’t hurt to add, “If now’s not a good time, it’s an offer with no expiry or agenda, just an excuse to get out of the office!” Sometimes a note of levity can bring a moment of relief to such an awful time. You can mention that this opportunity could be during work hours or outside them. Having a conversation after work can reduce the anxiety of feeling, “Well, we have to get back now.” 

Managers Have a Special Responsibility

When a manager has someone on their team who has experienced such a loss, the situation is different from that of a work colleague or acquaintance. As one of the corporate leaders I interviewed told me, “Managers have an obligation to intervene and offer both hard and soft resources.” 

Those could include internal and external support programs, as well as additional time off; temporary reassignment, especially if that person’s role involves travel;  and other gestures such as “What can I take off your plate right now?” 

As a mental health professional told me, “Managers are instrumental in helping to vector the person grieving to the appropriate resources, which also demonstrates a strong organizational duty of care and culture.” As studies demonstrate, a lack of “institutional care” can have a significant impact on a grieving person’s perception of support in the workplace. 

Be present, mindful, and delicate

As someone who is not a mental health professional, you can’t help another person make sense of something that makes no sense. But by being sensitive to the person’s grief in the aftermath of tragedy, you can open the door for them to reach out for companionship, comfort, and even help in finding support.  

And if that ask never comes from your colleague, as long as you were an empathetic listener, it’s not a failure on your part. After such a traumatic experience, each person’s grief narrative is different and it might or might not be something that involves workplace peers, friends, and colleagues. Yet by trying as best you can to follow these strategies, including empathetic listening and validating how your friend is coping, you can provide an opportunity for future interactions without the presumption and pressure that there might be one.  

This article does not constitute or imply mental health advice or counseling. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, call or text 988 or visit 988lifeline.org to connect with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, available 24/7 in the United States. If there is immediate danger, call 911. People grieving a suicide loss can find support groups, peer support, and other resources at afsp.org/ive-lost-someone/.

Thousands of the lasers could fit on a single chip, opening possibilities for more efficient data centers, smartphones, and advanced medical sensors.

items.title: [Pinterest Engineering Blog - Medium] Evolving Pinterest’s Embedding Retrieval Platform
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Authors: Bowen Zhou | Staff Software Engineer; Shan Gao | Senior Software Engineer; Jingwen Hu | Software Engineer II; Wenjiang Chu | Staff Software Engineer

The Billion-Embedding Challenge

At Pinterest, the “signal” is our lifeblood. Whether it’s a home decor enthusiast finding the perfect rug or a fashion seeker discovering a new aesthetic, our discovery engine relies on understanding deep semantic relationships to help our users find inspirations. Over the last few years, the explosive growth of embedding-based retrieval has fundamentally transformed how we surface these signals — and at the heart of that transformation is Manas, Pinterest’s in-house distributed search platform.

Embedding Retrieval is one of the core capabilities of Manas, supporting multiple approximate nearest neighbor search algorithms, hybrid queries with both token and embedding clauses, as well as real-time updates to ensure fresh contents become searchable within seconds. Deployed on over 80 clusters and serving billions of embeddings, Manas embedding retrieval powers all major product surfaces at Pinterest including Home Feed, Search, Related Pins, Ads, and Notifications.

However, as our corpus scales toward tens of billions of embeddings and our models capture increasingly complex interactions, we face mounting challenges around cost efficiency, scalability, and flexibility. On the infrastructure side, traditional ANN algorithms like HNSW are notoriously memory-hungry — they require the entire index to reside in RAM to maintain low query latency, making cost grow linearly with corpus size. On the modeling side, the classic two-tower retrieval paradigm is too restrictive: it reduces each candidate to a single embedding and scores relevance through a simple dot product, leaving little room to express richer, context-dependent notions of similarity.

To tackle these challenges, our team has been evolving Manas’s embedding retrieval stack across three fronts:

  • Quantization. We reduce the memory footprint of embedding indices by compressing vectors into lower-bit representations with fewer effective dimensions. Quantization has been rolled out to all major use cases, delivering over 50% memory reduction in embedding indices and 20–30% cost savings in serving infrastructure.
  • SSD-based Serving. Rather than holding entire indices in RAM, we serve ANN queries directly from SSD by carefully bounding the I/O per request — sustaining high throughput with low tail latencies at a fraction of the memory cost. Early experiments demonstrate a 10x reduction in memory usage and 40% CPU savings compared to in-memory serving
  • Multi-embedding Retrieval. We move beyond the single-vector-per-candidate constraint of the two-tower model by supporting richer scoring functions that consider multiple embeddings per candidate. This unlocks more expressive ranking at the retrieval stage. We are currently partnering with a product team to launch a pilot use case.

In this blog post, we will delve into the technical details and results of each initiative, and discuss what’s next for embedding retrieval in Manas.

Quantization: Redefining the Footprint of High-Recall Search

For a long time, serving embeddings in 16-bit or 32-bit float precision was considered the common practice. But at Pinterest’s scale, raw precision is a luxury that often provides diminishing returns. We discovered that quantization — transforming these high-dimensional float vectors into compact integer representations — is one of our most effective ways to better cost efficiency.

Evaluating the Trade-offs: SQ vs. PQ

In the Manas stack, we focused our implementation on two primary quantization algorithms: Scalar Quantization (SQ) and Product Quantization (PQ). The core of these methodologies lies in partitioning the vector space into disjoint subspaces and mapping each vector into an integer representation: SQ applies uniform discretization from float to integer per dimension, while PQ performs a K-Means clustering in each subspace and maps a subvector to the ID of the closest cluster centroid.

Benchmarks on a 100-million-embedding GraphSage dataset confirmed this intuition. We evaluated both SQ and PQ across two ANN algorithms (HNSW and IVF) and observed a clear trade-off: PQ achieves higher compression but with a significant recall decrease, while SQ delivers strong compression with minimal loss on recall.

  • PQ reduces the HNSW index by 74% and the IVF index by 93%, with a recall in the range of 70–80%
  • SQ reduces the HNSW index by 59% and the IVF index by 75%, with a recall over 90% consistently

Given the trade-off demonstrated by the offline benchmarking exercise, we ran online A/B experiments in production to select the best performing quantizer for each use case, and ensure negligible impact on user engagement metrics when enabling quantization. We launched SQ and PQ across major product use cases, reducing the total memory allocation significantly and realizing 20–30% cost savings for serving.

Technical Deep Dive: SIMD and Linear Scaling

Shifting to 8-bit or 4-bit representations isn’t just a memory win; it’s a compute challenge. Usually, SQ requires a decoding step before distance computation, which can become a CPU bottleneck. To solve this, we implemented Linear Scaling SQ, which quantizes a vector by scaling only, and thus eliminates the decoding step before distance computation. The key enabler here is SIMD intrinsics, which allows the CPU to perform multiple 8-bit integer operations with each instruction, and hence reduces the total computing resources needed per query by 10–15% in our use cases.

SSD Serving: Moving Beyond the Constraints of RAM

Our journey of improving embedding retrieval cost efficiency led us to exploring alternative ANN algorithms that take advantage of recent NVMe SSD performance advancements. The current generation of SSD devices are roughly an order of magnitude cheaper per gigabyte, but with the latency increased from nanoseconds to microseconds, which can slow down queries if I/O operations are not carefully managed. To bridge this gap, we experimented with I/O-aware ANN algorithms that were designed to minimize the number of random reads issued per query while retaining a recall score as good as memory-based algorithms.

DiskANN vs. SPANN

In our experiments, we benchmarked two disk-based ANN algorithms, DiskANN and SPANN, with a 100M-embedding corpus collected from a Pinterest Search use case. While DiskANN is a robust graph-based approach, SPANN emerged as the better option for the Manas use cases.

Our team’s key observation was applying PQ quantization to the on-disk embedding store while retaining the full precision centroids helped the search accuracy and throughput significantly — a slight tweak from the original SPANN paper. This makes SPANN+PQ 4.5x faster than plain SPANN and achieves over 3x the QPS of DiskANN with 1/3 the latency, with a slight 5% recall drop.

Implementing SPANN in Manas

We implemented the SPANN algorithm in Manas, which stores the centroid index in the memory and the large posting lists in the disk, and guarantees both disk-access efficiency (low latency) and high recall by effectively reducing the disk access number per request. In the index-building stage, we adopt the hierarchical balanced clustering algorithm from SPANN for selecting the centroids, which ensures evenly distributed cluster sizes, and hence similar lengths of posting lists to keep the tail latency low. We build the centroid index using HNSW, which is well-suited for in-memory search over a relatively small set of centroids. In a preliminary evaluation with a Pin recommendation use case that indexes over 5 billion embeddings, our SPANN implementation saves over 40% of CPU time for production queries when compared with HNSW, with a <5% recall drop. Our next step is to adopt SPANN across all major use cases.

Multi-Embedding Retrieval: The Shift Toward Late Interaction

As we improve cost efficiency, we are also evolving the expressivity of the Manas embedding retrieval stack. The traditional “Two-Tower” model, while efficient, collapses an entire Pin or query into a single vector, often losing the nuanced, token-level semantics that define high-quality discovery.

Contrast in Paradigms: Sum of MaxSim

We are now moving toward Late Interaction models , such as ColBERT. Unlike the single dot product of two-tower models, late interaction represents documents and queries as lists of vectors. We use the “Sum of MaxSim” scoring logic to capture the maximum similarity between each query token and the document’s tokens.

Integrating this into Manas required comprehensive changes in our serving stack. We integrated the multi-embedding retrieval as a new query type and updated Manas to handle multiple query embeddings rather than a single vector per query. This required updating the Manas query parser to understand these complex queries, as well as running multiple ANN searches from a multi-embedding query simultaneously. Currently, we are working with a client team to launch a pilot use case for the multi-embedding query support in Manas. This represents the next frontier of Pinterest search: moving from “two tower” to true model-based retrieval.

Looking Ahead

The future of vector search at Pinterest lies at the intersection of infrastructure efficiency and retrieval model innovation. Over the next five years, our central goal is to evolve Manas embedding retrieval into an architecture that is scalable, cost-efficient, and open to new retrieval paradigms. We are pursuing this along three directions: adopting SPANN and SPFresh to push CPU and memory costs even lower for billion-scale indices; building first-class support for multi-embedding retrieval models like ColBERT that enable richer, interaction-based scoring at the retrieval stage; and embracing GPU-based retrieval systems like SilverTorch and TIGER to unlock new model capabilities.

Acknowledgements

Many people from Core and Ads Delivery Infra teams contributed to the projects discussed in this blog post. Special thanks to Ellie Madsen, Jennifer Kong, and Jiawei Kuang for working on various Manas embedding retrieval projects. Thanks to our collaborators from client teams, including Bowen Deng, Jiaxing Qu, Ryan Hou, Minhazul Islam SK, Wei-Ting Lin, J.J. Hu, Konik Kothari, Yujiao Guo, Hanlin Lu, Bella Huang, Ai Zhang, Janvi Palan. Last but not least, many thanks to Van Lam, Tao Yang, Deeksha Sharma, Kartik Paramasivam, Abhishek Tayal, Zheng Liu for leadership support.

Evolving Pinterest’s Embedding Retrieval Platform was originally published in Pinterest Engineering Blog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
